questions.q: What problem does model parallelism solve that data parallelism cannot?
options: It speeds up data loading from disk
It allows training a model that is too large to fit on a single GPU, by splitting the model itself across devices
It removes the need for an optimizer
It eliminates the need for gradient computation
questions.explain: Data parallelism replicates the full model on every GPU, which fails when the model itself doesn't fit on one GPU. Model parallelism splits the model's structure across devices instead.

questions.q: In tensor parallelism, what happens when a column-parallel layer's output feeds into a row-parallel layer?
options: Nothing -- no communication is needed between the two layers
Each GPU's partial output must be combined via an all-reduce across the tensor-parallel group before the next operation can proceed
The entire model is re-synchronized from a checkpoint
The row-parallel layer is skipped entirely
questions.explain: Because each GPU only holds a slice of the layer's weight matrix, partial results must be combined with an all-reduce (or all-gather) to reconstruct the correct full output, and this happens inside every layer, many times per step.

questions.q: Why does tensor parallelism require a much faster interconnect than pipeline parallelism?
options: Tensor parallelism uses more GPU memory per device

Tensor parallelism requires communication inside every layer's forward and backward pass, many times per step, while pipeline parallelism only needs point-to-point hand-offs between neighboring stages
Tensor parallelism only works on a single GPU
Pipeline parallelism does not require any network at all
questions.explain: Tensor parallelism's frequent in-layer all-reduces are far more communication-intensive than pipeline parallelism's neighbor-only activation hand-offs, so tensor parallelism needs fast interconnects like NVLink within a server.

questions.q: What is the 'pipeline bubble' in pipeline parallelism, and what reduces it?
options: A memory leak caused by too many layers; reduced by fewer stages
GPU idle time caused by stages waiting on each other sequentially; reduced by splitting the batch into smaller micro-batches fed through the pipeline in sequence
A network error that halts training; reduced by restarting the job
An artifact of mixed precision training; reduced by using fp32 only
questions.explain: Without micro-batching, each stage waits idle for the previous stage to finish the whole batch. Micro-batching keeps more stages busy simultaneously by feeding smaller pieces of the batch through in sequence.

questions.q: In practice, how are tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism typically combined in large-scale training?
options: They are never combined -- only one is used per training job
Tensor parallelism is used within a server (fast NVLink), and pipeline parallelism is used across servers (slower inter-node network)
Pipeline parallelism is used within a server, and tensor parallelism is used across servers
Both are always applied to the exact same layers simultaneously
questions.explain: Because tensor parallelism's frequent communication needs a fast interconnect, it's used within a server where NVLink is available, while pipeline parallelism's lighter point-to-point hand-offs can tolerate the slower network between servers.
